plan-of-saint-gall.name: Plan of Saint Gall
plan-of-saint-gall.summary: A medieval architectural drawing from 820–830 AD depicting an entire Benedictine monastery, never actually built, and the only surviving major architectural drawing from that 700-year period.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

capitulare-de-villis.name: Capitulare de villis
capitulare-de-villis.summary: A late 8th- or early 9th-century text, likely from Charlemagne's reign, setting rules for managing royal estates, including land, animals, justice and administration.

ottonian-dynasty.name: Ottonian Dynasty
ottonian-dynasty.summary: A Saxon dynasty of German monarchs and Holy Roman emperors that ruled from 919 to 1024, named for Otto the Great, credited with making Germany Europe's leading kingdom.

reichenau-abbey.name: Reichenau Abbey
reichenau-abbey.summary: A Benedictine monastery founded in 724 on an island in southern Germany by Saint Pirmin, who had fled Visigothic Spain, with patronage from Charles Martel and local Alemannian rulers.

carolingian-art.name: Carolingian art
carolingian-art.summary: Art produced in the Frankish Empire from about 780 to 900 under Charlemagne and his heirs, blending classical Mediterranean styles with Northern traditions and paving the way for Romanesque art.

gero-cross.name: Gero Cross
gero-cross.summary: A crucifix of around 965-970 in Cologne Cathedral, the oldest large sculpture of the crucified Christ north of the Alps, commissioned by Archbishop Gero.

cologne-cathedral.name: Cologne Cathedral
cologne-cathedral.summary: A Gothic Catholic cathedral in Cologne, Germany, begun in 1248 and only completed in 1880, and the tallest twin-spired church in the world.

otto-the-great.name: Otto the Great
otto-the-great.summary: East Frankish king from 936 and Holy Roman Emperor from 962 to 973, who unified the German duchies, defeated the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955, and was crowned emperor by Pope John XII.

imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.name: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire
imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.summary: Octagonal coronation crown of the Holy Roman Emperor, probably made in the late 10th century and used until the empire's dissolution in 1806; now kept in Vienna.
imperial-crown-of-the-holy-roman-empire.source_title: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire

cross-of-lothair.name: Cross of Lothair
cross-of-lothair.summary: A jewelled processional cross made around 1000 AD, probably in Cologne, considered an outstanding example of Ottonian goldsmith's work held in the Aachen Cathedral Treasury.

dendrochronology.name: Dendrochronology
dendrochronology.summary: The scientific method of dating tree rings to the exact year they formed, useful for precise dating too recent for radiocarbon methods and for calibrating them.

otto-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Otto II
otto-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 973 to 983, of the Ottonian dynasty, who continued his father Otto the Great's policies of strengthening imperial rule and expanding into southern Italy.

essen-minster.name: Essen Minster
essen-minster.summary: A Gothic cathedral in Essen, Germany, that grew out of a collegiate abbey founded around 845; its surviving octagonal westwork is a rare example of Ottonian pre-Romanesque architecture.

palatine-chapel-aachen.name: Palatine Chapel, Aachen
palatine-chapel-aachen.summary: An early medieval chapel, the surviving core of Charlemagne's palace at Aachen, which later hosted royal coronations from 936 to 1531.

pendilia.name: Pendilia
pendilia.summary: Hanging pendants or ornaments attached to crowns and other Early Medieval metalwork, commonly shown on Byzantine coins and worn on imperial crowns from Marcian onward.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

basilica-of-san-vitale.name: San Vitale in Ravenna
basilica-of-san-vitale.summary: A 6th-century church in Ravenna, Italy, an important surviving example of early Byzantine art, famed for mosaics including a portrait of Emperor Justinian I.

pannonian-avars.name: Pannonian Avars
pannonian-avars.summary: A confederation of Eurasian nomads who built the Avar Khaganate in the Carpathian Basin from the late 6th to early 9th centuries, known for invasions of the Byzantine Empire and influence on Slavic migrations.

gniezno.name: Gniezno
gniezno.summary: A Polish city that was the first historical capital of Poland in the 10th and early 11th centuries and remains the country's ecclesiastical capital.

pope-leo-iii.name: Pope Leo III
pope-leo-iii.summary: Bishop of Rome and leader of the Papal States from 795 to 816, protected by Charlemagne and famous for crowning him emperor.

kingdom-of-italy-holy-roman-empire.name: Kingdom of Italy (Holy Roman Empire)
kingdom-of-italy-holy-roman-empire.summary: A constituent kingdom of the Holy Roman Empire covering northern and central Italy, ruled from Pavia, whose crown Otto I of Germany seized in 951 before his imperial coronation in 962.

pavia.name: Pavia
pavia.summary: A town in Lombardy, Northern Italy, that served as capital of the Ostrogothic Kingdom, then the Kingdom of the Lombards, then the Kingdom of Italy across the medieval period.

nowa-huta.name: Nowa Huta
nowa-huta.summary: A district of Kraków, Poland, with more than 200,000 residents, built as one of the largest planned socialist-realist settlements in the world, with layout echoing Paris or London.

bonikowo.name: Bonikowo
bonikowo.summary: A village in Kościan County, in west-central Poland's Greater Poland Voivodeship.

bruszczewo.name: Bruszczewo
bruszczewo.summary: Village in west-central Poland's Kościan County, where archaeologists have found early medieval weapons and utensils.

old-high-german.name: Old High German
old-high-german.summary: The earliest stage of the German language, spanning roughly 500/750 to 1050 CE, preserved mainly in religious texts composed in monasteries.

hildebrandslied.name: Hildebrandslied
hildebrandslied.summary: The earliest poetic text in German, an Old High German heroic verse about a father and son who fail to recognize each other before fighting, written down in the 830s.

muspilli.name: Muspilli
muspilli.summary: A ninth-century Old High German alliterative poem, surviving in 103 incomplete lines, describing the soul's fate after death and at the Last Judgment.

old-high-german-literature.name: Old High German literature
old-high-german-literature.summary: Literature written in Old High German from the 8th to mid-11th century, produced almost entirely in monasteries and religious in nature.

middle-high-german-literature.name: Middle High German literature
middle-high-german-literature.summary: German literature written between the mid-11th and mid-14th centuries, including a 'golden age' around 1170–1230 of courtly love poetry, Arthurian romance and heroic epic.

cyril-and-methodius.name: Cyril and Methodius
cyril-and-methodius.summary: Byzantine Christian brothers (826–869 and 815–885) known as the 'Apostles to the Slavs' for devising the Glagolitic alphabet and evangelizing the early Slavic peoples.

great-moravia.name: Great Moravia
great-moravia.summary: The first major West Slavic state in Central Europe, where Saints Cyril and Methodius introduced Slavic literacy after 863; it peaked under Svatopluk I and collapsed around 906.

glagolitic-script.name: Glagolitic script
glagolitic-script.summary: The oldest-known Slavic alphabet, created in the 9th century by the monk Cyril to translate Greek scripture into Old Church Slavonic, later largely replaced by Cyrillic.

otfrid-of-weissenburg.name: Otfrid of Weissenburg
otfrid-of-weissenburg.summary: A monk at Weissenburg abbey (c. 800–after 870) who wrote the Evangelienbuch, an Old High German rhymed gospel poem, and is the earliest named German poet.

heliand.name: Heliand
heliand.summary: A 9th-century epic poem in Old Saxon retelling the life of Jesus in Germanic alliterative verse; the largest surviving work of written Old Saxon.

ibrahim-ibn-yaqub.name: Ibrahim ibn Yaqub
ibrahim-ibn-yaqub.summary: A 10th-century Andalusi Jewish traveler from Tortosa, esteemed for his knowledge of science, medicine and geography, who journeyed through Europe for the Umayyad Caliph of Córdoba and wrote an account of the peoples he encountered.

treaty-of-verdun.name: Treaty of Verdun
treaty-of-verdun.summary: Agreement of 10 August 843 that divided the Carolingian Empire among the three surviving sons of Louis I, ending a civil war and starting the empire's breakup.

kingdom-of-germany.name: Kingdom of Germany
kingdom-of-germany.summary: The core medieval realm of the Holy Roman Empire, formed from the eastern Frankish kingdom after the 843 Treaty of Verdun, whose kings claimed the imperial title from 962 onward.

charles-the-fat.name: Charles the Fat
charles-the-fat.summary: Carolingian emperor from 881 to 887 and great-grandson of Charlemagne; the last legitimate Carolingian to rule a reunited Frankish empire, he was deposed in a coup in 887.

regino-of-pr-m.name: Regino of Prüm
regino-of-pr-m.summary: A Benedictine monk who died in 915, serving as abbot of Prüm and later of Saint Martin's at Trier, whose chronicle is a key source for late Carolingian history.

berengar-i-of-italy.name: Berengar I of Italy
berengar-i-of-italy.summary: King of Italy from 887 and Holy Roman Emperor from 915 to 924, whose 36-year reign faced seven rival claimants and Magyar raids.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.name: Kingdom of the Lombards
kingdom-of-the-lombards.summary: An early medieval state founded by the Germanic Lombards in Italy in the late 500s CE, ruled from Pavia, that opposed the Byzantine Empire until Charlemagne conquered it in 774.

duchy-of-rome.name: Duchy of Rome
duchy-of-rome.summary: A Byzantine-ruled state within the Exarchate of Ravenna, often at odds with the Papacy, which ceased to function as an administrative unit after the Papal States formed in 756.

adelaide-of-italy.name: Adelaide of Italy
adelaide-of-italy.summary: Holy Roman Empress (931–999) by marriage to Otto the Great, crowned in Rome in 962; later regent of the empire for her grandson from 991 to 995, and a model for future royal consorts.

samo.name: Samo
samo.summary: Founder and ruler, from 623 to 658, of the first recorded unified Slavic tribal polity, later called Samo's realm; the earliest source says he was a Frankish merchant.

svatopluk-i-of-moravia.name: Svatopluk I
svatopluk-i-of-moravia.summary: Ruler of Great Moravia (870-894) under whom the state reached its greatest territorial extent; he defeated Frankish invaders and was even addressed as "King" by Pope Stephen V in 885.

hungarians.name: Magyars
hungarians.summary: An ethnic group native to Hungary and the Carpathian Basin, numbering about 14.5 million worldwide, sharing a common Uralic language, culture and history.

carantania.name: Carantania
carantania.summary: A Slavic principality that arose in the late 7th century in what is now southern Austria and northeastern Slovenia, becoming a Frankish vassal before losing its autonomy by 828.

salian-franks.name: Salian Franks
salian-franks.summary: A Frankish people first recorded in the 4th century after settling in the Roman Rhine delta; later rulers of northern France, including the Merovingian dynasty, were traditionally seen as their descendants.

ripuarian-franks.name: Ripuarian Franks
ripuarian-franks.summary: Franks who settled around Roman-era Cologne on the Rhine, traditionally treated as one of two major Frankish groups alongside the Salian Franks, though the tribal origin of the name is now debated.

saxons.name: Saxons
saxons.summary: A Germanic people of early medieval northern Germany, led by the semi-legendary Widukind before Charlemagne conquered them in the Saxon Wars (772–804) and forced their conversion to Christianity.

bavarians.name: Bavarians
bavarians.summary: An ethnic group of Germans native to Bavaria, traditionally Catholic, whose dialect and identity trace back to the historic Electorate of Bavaria.

swabians.name: Swabians
swabians.summary: A German ethnic group native to Swabia, in what is now southwestern Germany, descended from the Alemanni and the medieval Duchy of Swabia.

conrad-iii-of-germany.name: Conrad III
conrad-iii-of-germany.summary: King of the Romans in the Holy Roman Empire from 1138 to 1152, of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, who led German forces in the failed Second Crusade.

henry-the-fowler.name: Henry the Fowler
henry-the-fowler.summary: Duke of Saxony from 912 and king of East Francia from 919 to 936, considered the founder of the medieval German state and its first non-Frankish king.

utrecht.name: Utrecht
utrecht.summary: The fourth-largest city in the Netherlands, a religious centre since the 8th century, where the 1579 Union of Utrecht laid the groundwork for the Dutch Republic.

zutphen.name: Zutphen
zutphen.summary: A city in the Dutch province of Gelderland, about 30 km northeast of Arnhem, first mentioned in the 11th century; its name likely means "south fen".

deventer.name: Deventer
deventer.summary: One of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, on the river IJssel, first mentioned in 9th-century sources and granted city rights in 1123.

aachen.name: Aachen
aachen.summary: A German city near the Belgian and Dutch borders that became the main royal residence of the Frankish Empire under Charlemagne around 800 CE and the coronation site of 31 Holy Roman Emperors.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

rabanus-maurus.name: Rabanus Maurus
rabanus-maurus.summary: A Frankish Benedictine monk who became archbishop of Mainz and wrote an influential encyclopedia, education treatises and Bible commentaries, earning him the title 'teacher of Germany' during the Carolingian age.

gottschalk-of-orbais.name: Gottschalk of Orbais
gottschalk-of-orbais.summary: A 9th-century Saxon monk and theologian (c. 808–868) whose doctrine of double predestination was condemned as heresy, leading to his monastic confinement for the rest of his life.

predestination.name: Double predestination
predestination.summary: A Christian theological doctrine, rooted in Augustine of Hippo's teaching that salvation comes from God's grace, holding that God has chosen some individuals for salvation and others for damnation.

carolingian-renaissance.name: Carolingian Renaissance
carolingian-renaissance.summary: A revival of learning, writing, and the arts in the Carolingian Empire under Charlemagne and his successors, drawing inspiration from ancient Roman, Greek, and Christian culture.

alcuin.name: Alcuin of York
alcuin.summary: Anglo-Saxon scholar and teacher (c. 735–804) from York who led Charlemagne's court school and helped shape the Carolingian Renaissance.

princely-abbey-of-fulda.name: Abbey of Fulda
princely-abbey-of-fulda.summary: A Benedictine abbey founded in 744, later granted imperial territory in 1221 making its abbots princes of the Holy Roman Empire; it became a prominent center of learning.

peter-of-pisa.name: Peter of Pisa
peter-of-pisa.summary: Italian grammarian, deacon and poet (744–799) summoned to Charlemagne's court in 776, where he served as the emperor's primary Latin teacher.

john-scotus-eriugena.name: John Scotus Eriugena
john-scotus-eriugena.summary: Irish Neoplatonist philosopher, theologian and poet (c.800–877), called the most original philosopher of the Carolingian era, known for his work Periphyseon.

pseudo-dionysius-the-areopagite.name: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite
pseudo-dionysius-the-areopagite.summary: Pseudonym of a Syrian or Greek monk and Neoplatonic theologian writing around 485 to 528 AD, who claimed to be a 1st-century disciple of Paul the Apostle; his mystical theology later shaped Christian thought.

paschasius-radbertus.name: Paschasius Radbertus
paschasius-radbertus.summary: A Carolingian theologian and abbot of Corbie monastery, best known for his 831 treatise on the Eucharist, later canonized in 1073.

carolingian-empire.name: Carolingian Empire
carolingian-empire.summary: A Frankish-led empire in Western and Central Europe from 800 to 887, begun when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Roman emperor; it later split into separate kingdoms.

pope-john-xii.name: Pope John XII
pope-john-xii.summary: Bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States from 955 to 964, possibly elected as young as 17, who crowned Otto I emperor and is widely seen as one of history's worst popes.

dorestad.name: Dorestad
dorestad.summary: An early medieval trading port in what is now the Netherlands that flourished in the 8th and early 9th centuries as a hub linking the Rhine, England, and Scandinavia.

louis-the-german.name: Louis the German
louis-the-german.summary: First king of East Francia (843–876) and grandson of Charlemagne, whose kingdom gave rise to the name Germany after his death.

frankish-language.name: Old Frankish
frankish-language.summary: West Germanic language spoken by the Franks from the 4th to 8th century, poorly recorded and mostly reconstructed from loanwords in Old French and Old Dutch.

old-dutch.name: Old Dutch
old-dutch.summary: The earliest stage of the Dutch language, spoken by descendants of the Salian Franks from about the 6th to 12th century before evolving into Middle Dutch.

austrasia.name: Austrasia
austrasia.summary: The northeastern realm of the early medieval Frankish kingdom, centred between the Meuse, Moselle, Rhine and Main rivers, founded under Merovingian king Clovis I.

neustria.name: Neustria
neustria.summary: The western part of the early medieval Frankish kingdom, centered on Paris, Orléans, Tours and Soissons, in contrast to the eastern sub-kingdom of Austrasia.
